coffees.name: Thailand Lanna Law Wu Natural
coffees.origin: Law Wu village, Chiang Mai highlands, Thailand
coffees.station: Law Wu village · Lanna Coffee & ITDF co-op
coffees.processNote: Whole cherries are dried in the sun with the fruit still on the bean, so the seed soaks in its own fruit sugar for weeks. That is where the ripe red fruit and the melon sweetness come from. The village's consistent shade slows ripening at 1,700 meters, which keeps the cup clean instead of wild.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Thailand is not where most people think their coffee comes from, and that is exactly why this cup is worth your attention. Law Wu is a village of the Lahu tribe, an indigenous people who came south out of China generations ago, perched at 1,700 meters in the mountains above Chiang Mai. Coffee has only grown here about fifteen years, but the cool air, constant shade, and strange beautiful terrain turn out to be nearly perfect for it. The partnership started in 2017 with four farmers. Their work was so consistent that five more joined, and today nine families grow some of the most interesting microlots in Southeast Asia.

Lanna Coffee exists to serve the hill tribes of Northern Thailand, communities of refugees who fled upheaval in China and Southeast Asia and have lived stateless and poor for over a century. Working with the Integrated Tribal Development Foundation, they helped build Thailand's first certified fair trade coffee co-op, now over 40 villages strong, with more than 400 coffee farms that are 100 percent farmer owned, growing single-source, pesticide-free coffee. Every bag helps another farmer convert to a crop that pays a stable living. A better life through a cup of coffee is a slow thing, but it is real.

journey.label: Law Wu · Chiang Mai highlands, Thailand
journey.story: Most coffee maps skip Thailand entirely. Up here in the mountains north of Chiang Mai, the Lahu village of Law Wu is quietly correcting that, nine farm families growing shade-slowed coffee at 1,700 meters on slopes where opium poppies grew a generation ago. To the northwest the limestone wall of Doi Luang Chiang Dao climbs out of the forest.

lookArounds.label: Walk old Chiang Mai
lookArounds.note: Tha Phae Gate and the brick walls of old Chiang Mai, the northern capital this coffee comes down the mountain to. The moat around the old city is 700 years old. Drag to look around; the arrows walk the streets.

lookArounds.label: Stand at Doi Suthep
lookArounds.note: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep, the golden temple on the mountain above Chiang Mai. Legend says a white elephant carrying a relic of the Buddha climbed up here, trumpeted three times, and chose this spot. One local-shot 360 from the terrace.

coffees.name: Rwanda Dukunde Kawa Mbilima Organic
coffees.processNote: Cherries are pulped the day they are picked, fermented in water, washed clean, and dried slowly on raised beds at the Musasa mill. The washed process strips the fruit away early, so what you taste is the bean itself and the high hills it grew on: clean, chocolaty, with fruit riding over the top.
coffees.aboutFarm:
This coffee comes from family farms gathered around the Musasa mill in the Gakenke district of Rwanda's Northern Province, up near a mountain gorilla habitat. The farm plots are so small that nobody measures them in acres; they are measured by the number of trees. Each family brings its cherry down the hill to the cooperative's wet mill, where it is sorted, washed, and dried with the kind of care you can only give coffee when you know every tree personally.

The farmers are members of the Dukunde Kawa Cooperative, a name that means roughly 'let's love coffee' in Kinyarwanda. They started in 2000 with just enough money to build one wet mill. Today they run four wet mills and their own dry mill, and more than 80 percent of the cooperative's workforce is women. Earnings have gone into livestock, healthcare, and programs to protect the land, which is to say the coffee is improving the hills it grows on.

journey.label: Musasa mill · Gakenke, Rwanda
journey.story: Rwanda is called the land of a thousand hills and this is deep in them. Around the Musasa mill in Gakenke district the farm plots are so small they are counted in trees, not acres, and most of the hands working the cooperative belong to women. Northwest along the horizon stand the Virunga volcanoes, the last home of the mountain gorillas.

lookArounds.label: Enter the gorilla park
lookArounds.note: The lower slopes of Mount Bisoke in Volcanoes National Park, a couple hours northwest of the mill. The bamboo and hagenia forests up here are home to the mountain gorillas, and this is where the treks to find them begin. One local-shot 360 from the mountain.

lookArounds.label: Climb to Karisoke
lookArounds.note: The high saddle between Mount Karisimbi and Mount Bisoke, where Dian Fossey built the Karisoke research camp in 1967 and spent 18 years living among the gorillas. She is buried up here beside them. One local-shot 360 from the trail.

coffees.name: El Salvador Peña Redonda Pacamara
coffees.processNote: Pacamara is El Salvador's own giant-bean variety, a cross of Pacas and Maragogipe, and the Lemus family handles it the traditional way: picked selectively at full ripeness, fully washed, and sun-dried during the dry season that conveniently arrives right at harvest. Stony soil and sweetgum shade slow the ripening, which is where the depth comes from.
coffees.aboutFarm:
Peña Redonda is named for the enormous round rock that dominates the farm, high above La Palma in Chalatenango. Carlos Mauricio Lemus Landaverde took the farm over after the death of his father, José María Lemus, and kept the family habits that built its reputation: clean processing and picking only what is ripe. The trees grow between 1,450 and 1,500 meters in stony soil under sweetgum shade, and the results speak at the national level. Their lots have placed at the Cup of Excellence four times, including 7th in the whole country in 2019, with an award profile of Swiss chocolate, orange, and peach.

Chalatenango, the 'valley of water and sand,' holds the highest ground in El Salvador, topping out at Cerro El Pital at 2,730 meters. For decades the famous Salvadoran coffees came from the west, until a La Palma farm took 1st place at the 2007 Cup of Excellence and put this region on the map for good. El Salvador is the birthplace of the Pacas and Pacamara varieties, and up here, where cool microclimates ripen the cherry slowly, Pacamara shows what it was born to do.

journey.label: Peña Redonda · La Palma, El Salvador
journey.story: La Palma hangs in the mountains of Chalatenango near the Honduran border, in what Salvadorans call the valley of water and sand. Peña Redonda is named for the great round rock on the property, where Pacamara ripens slowly in stony soil under sweetgum shade. Northeast of here the ridge climbs to Cerro El Pital, the highest point in the country.

lookArounds.label: Walk the murals of La Palma
lookArounds.note: La Palma, the mountain town below the farm, famous across El Salvador for the bright painted murals in the style of Fernando Llort that cover its walls. One local-shot 360 from the middle of town.

lookArounds.label: Stand on Cerro El Pital
lookArounds.note: Cerro El Pital, the highest point in El Salvador at 2,730 meters, on the Honduran border just past the farm. Up here the cloud forest drips with fog most mornings. One local-shot 360 near the summit.

coldBrew.name: One Batch Cold Brew
coldBrew.aboutFarm:
Origin TBD, but it'll be something worth the wait. Steeped 18 to 24 hours, half a gallon of water to 220 grams of grounds, a ratio strong enough that you're meant to dilute it rather than wonder where the flavor went. What comes out the other end is thick and dark, closer to a concentrate than a coffee, even though nobody around here calls it that.

Cut it with cream and a splash of water if you want it easy. A touch of sweetener if that's your thing, no judgment. Or pour it straight over ice, no water, no cream, and let it hit the way it's supposed to. That's how I drink the first glass of every batch, standing at the counter, deciding if this one's a keeper.

Brewed once, one batch, by the half gallon. When it's gone, it's gone until the next one.
